title: {{NAME}} and the Three Gifts
moral: The most meaningful gifts are the ones that reveal who you truly are.

pages.content:
In the kingdom of Lumen Vale, there was a tradition: when a child came of age, they received three gifts, one from each of the realm's great powers.

A gift from the Princess (on behalf of the human realm). A gift from the Fairy High Council (on behalf of the magical realm). A gift from the unicorn elders (on behalf of the ancient realm).

The gifts were chosen by the givers based on what they perceived in the recipient.

{{NAME}}'s ceremony was scheduled for a Tuesday, which felt ordinary for something this significant.

pages.content:
Princess Sorrel gave him a notebook bound in deep blue leather.

"You see what others miss," she said, formally. "And you make sure it is not lost. This is for everything you will notice."

The head fairy gave him a lens no bigger than a thumbnail, set in a silver frame.

"It shows things as they are, not as they appear," she said. "For when the truth is obscured."

Then the unicorn elder came forward.

She was the oldest creature {{NAME}} had ever stood near: her horn pure white, her coat the colour of old stone.

She lowered her horn.

pages.content:
When the unicorn's horn touched his forehead, he saw three things.

First: himself, as he was. Exactly.

Second: himself, as he was becoming.

Third: something he couldn't quite see yet, a direction rather than a picture, a feeling rather than an image.

The elder raised her horn.

"Her gift," said the head fairy quietly, "is the gift of knowing your own path."

{{NAME}} stood very still for a moment.

Then he said: "Thank you." He meant all three of them.

pages.content:
After the ceremony, Princess Sorrel asked him what he had seen.

"Myself," he said. "Three times, three ways."

"Was it frightening?"

"No," he said. "It was clarifying."

The head fairy, overhearing, made a sound like small bells.

"That is the correct response," she said. "Some people are frightened by their own reflection. You were interested."

"I was always going to be interested," said {{NAME}}.

All three of them looked at him.

"We know," said the princess. "That's why we were there."

pages.content:
He walked home with the notebook, the lens, and the memory of the horn's touch.

He tried the lens on the way: held it up to the evening sky.

The stars through it were clearer and more numerous than he had ever seen them, and between the known constellations were faint configurations he had never been shown.

He put it away carefully.

In bed, the notebook on the table and the lens beside it, he lay in the dark and thought about the third thing he'd seen: the direction.

He closed his eyes and faced it.

He fell asleep going that way.
